trace.msg: Let's look at this puzzle carefully. I'll only move when I can explain why.
I can't rule out left, down or up yet, so I'll make an educated guess: left.
Going left would leave number 3 unreachable without crossing a higher number; going around the edge to (1,3), every way of continuing runs into a dead end within a few moves. So the line goes right.

Contradiction! Every way forward fails: going around the edge to (1,4), every way of continuing runs into a dead end within a few moves; going right, every way of continuing runs into a dead end within a few moves. So my guess (left from number 1) was wrong. Next I'll try down.
I can't rule out left, around the edge to (1,4) or right yet, so I'll make an educated guess: left.

Going left would leave number 3 unreachable without crossing a higher number; going around the edge to (1,3) would force the two-exit cells to link up into a loop (or put the numbers out of order). So the line goes up.
Number 3 is next and right here, so the line takes it.
Going left would leave number 4 unreachable without crossing a higher number. So the line goes right.
I can't rule out right or up yet, so I'll make an educated guess: right.
Number 4 is next and right here, so the line takes it.
Going down, every way of continuing runs into a dead end within a few moves. So the line goes right.
Number 5 is only reachable this way.
The line must go up: around the edge to (4,1) is number 10, which comes later.
I can't rule out up or around the edge to (2,1) yet, so I'll make an educated guess: up.

Going around the edge to (1,1) would leave number 6 unreachable without crossing a higher number; going left, the next move is forced and the line gets stuck at cell (6,5). So the line goes around the edge to (6,6).
The line must go left: around the edge to (6,1) is number 11, which comes later.
Going left would force the two-exit cells to link up into a loop (or put the numbers out of order). So the line goes down.
The line must go left: down is number 15, which comes later.
Cell (1,4) has only two exits, so the line must pass through it now: it goes up.
Only one free cell next to the line, so it goes left.
Number 8 is only reachable this way.
Going left would leave number 9 unreachable without crossing a higher number. So the line goes around the edge to (6,2).
Number 9 is next and right here, so the line takes it.
Going left would force the line onto number 11 before its turn. So the line goes up.
Number 10 is only reachable this way.
The line must go down: up is number 12, which comes later.
Every cell is covered and the numbers are in order. Case closed!
I grow a search tree: my policy network suggests moves, a trained value head judge them. 48 simulations per move.
One of my simulated futures reached the end after 9 simulations. Following it!
Let evolution do the work: 24 random lines compete, the fittest breed and mutate.
Generation 0: the best random line covers 15/36 cells (42%).
Generation 5: fitness 14/36. The best line covers 15 cells, the first 14 of them still look solvable.
Generation 9: fitness 23/36. The best line covers 27 cells, the first 23 of them still look solvable.
Generation 10: fitness 36/36. The best line covers 36 cells.
Generation 10: a perfect line evolved! Every cell covered.
Feeling lucky! Before every move I'll play 24 random futures and bet on the move that survives most often.
Tried 72 futures: 88% survive going down (best covers 64%); left 88%; up 4%.
Tried 72 futures: 92% survive going left (best covers 64%); around the edge to (1,4) 83%; right 67%.
Jackpot! A future after going up covers the whole board. Cashing in!
Let x(cell, step) mean 'this cell is step number <step> of the line'. 36 cells x 36 steps, minus everything that's impossible at a glance.
